opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that s1 roughly matches o1-preview on the reasoning benchmarks we focused on, and on some of them it actually goes a bit beyond it. The main ones we looked at were competition math, so AIME 2024 and MATH500, and then GPQA Diamond for PhD-level science questions. On AIME in particular, with budget forcing, where we let the model think longer by appending "Wait" when it tries to stop, we saw it climb past o1-preview. I believe the gain over o1-preview on competition math was up to around 27%.

But I want to be careful about what that does and doesn't mean. We're not claiming s1 is better than o1 in general. o1-preview is a much broader system, and the full o1 model is stronger than s1 on these benchmarks. What's interesting to me is how little it took. s1 is Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct fine-tuned on just a thousand carefully selected reasoning examples, which we chose for quality, difficulty, and diversity. The training took something like 26 minutes on 16 H100s. So the point is less "we beat OpenAI" and more that a lot of this reasoning capability seems to already be latent in a strong base model, and you can unlock it really cheaply.

The other part I'm excited about is the test-time scaling curve. We can control how long the model thinks, and performance improves as you give it more thinking tokens, which is the behavior o1 showed but didn't explain publicly. Being able to reproduce that with a very simple, fully open recipe, with open weights, data, and code, is what I'd emphasize. That said, the scaling does flatten out eventually. If you force it to keep going for too long, it starts looping or repeating itself, so there's still a lot of room to improve how we extrapolate test-time compute.

fable-5.1.text:
So, to be clear about what we were actually trying to do: s1 was never meant to be a model that beats o1-preview across the board. The goal was to find the simplest possible recipe that gives you test-time scaling and strong reasoning performance, and then to see how close that simple recipe gets you to something like o1-preview. And the answer turned out to be: surprisingly close, with a tiny fraction of the data and compute.

Concretely, we took Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, fine-tuned it on just 1,000 carefully selected questions with reasoning traces, and added this budget forcing trick where we control how long the model thinks at inference time. On the competition math benchmarks, s1-32B actually exceeds o1-preview. On AIME24 it's a bit above o1-preview, and on MATH500 it's in the same range or slightly higher. On GPQA Diamond, which is the harder science questions, we're a little below o1-preview, but still in the same neighborhood.

So the way I'd frame it is: on math, we match or exceed it; on broader scientific reasoning, we're close but not quite there. And we're very clearly below o1 proper, and below things like DeepSeek-R1 and the r1 distills, which were trained on hundreds of thousands of reasoning examples. That's the honest picture. Those models used orders of magnitude more data, and if you train on 800,000 samples instead of 1,000, you should expect better numbers.

What I find most interesting isn't the raw comparison but the sample efficiency. The 1,000 examples matter a lot more than you'd think, and the selection process was really the key: we filtered from about 59,000 candidate questions down to 1,000 based on quality, difficulty, and diversity. When we ablated that and just trained on random samples or on the full 59K, the random 1K was much worse, and the full set only gave marginal gains over our 1K. So most of the value is in picking the right questions, not in volume.

And then the test-time scaling piece: with budget forcing, where we literally append "Wait" when the model tries to stop, we get a clean curve where more thinking tokens gives you better accuracy, up to a point. That's the behavior people were excited about with o1, and we got it with what is essentially supervised fine-tuning that takes about 26 minutes on 16 H100s.

So, to summarize: competitive with o1-preview on math, somewhat behind on science, well behind the frontier models. But it tells you that a lot of the reasoning capability is already in the base model, and you need very little to unlock it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about calling S1 better than o1-preview across the board. On the math benchmarks we evaluated, it’s competitive, and on some it outperforms o1-preview. But those are specific evaluations, not a comprehensive comparison of everything the models can do.

The interesting result is that we can get there with a relatively simple approach: fine-tuning a strong base model on just 1,000 carefully selected examples, then controlling how much it thinks at inference time. That doesn’t mean we built those capabilities from scratch with 1,000 examples—the base model already contributes a lot. It shows how much you can unlock with a small amount of high-quality reasoning data and additional test-time compute.
